title: 405. Trigonometry & Periodic Models: Converting Radians to Degrees
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Size of one radian in degrees
questions.learningObjective: Estimate the degree measure of one radian.
questions.question: Approximately how many degrees is \(1\) radian?
questions.explanation: Since \(\pi\) radians is \(180^\circ\), one radian is \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\approx\frac{180^\circ}{3.1416}\approx 57.3^\circ\). The number \(0.0175\) is the radian measure of \(1^\circ\), which is the opposite conversion.
questions.hint: Use the fact that \(\pi\) radians equals \(180^\circ\) and divide both sides by \(\pi\).

questions.learningObjective: Convert a standard radian measure to degrees.
questions.question: What is the degree measure of \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians?
questions.explanation: Multiply by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\): \(\frac{\pi}{6}\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=\frac{180^\circ}{6}=30^\circ\). The measure \(60^\circ\) corresponds to \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) radians.

questions.concept: Converting a radian measure in the second quadrant
questions.learningObjective: Convert a multiple of pi over three to degrees.
questions.question: What is the degree measure of \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) radians?
questions.explanation: Multiply by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\): \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=\frac{360^\circ}{3}=120^\circ\). The measure \(150^\circ\) corresponds to \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) radians.
questions.hint: Since \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) radians is one third of a half turn, find that value first and then double it.

questions.concept: Converting a radian measure beyond a half turn
questions.learningObjective: Convert a radian measure greater than pi to degrees.
questions.question: What is the degree measure of \(\frac{5\pi}{4}\) radians?
questions.explanation: Multiply by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\): \(\frac{5\pi}{4}\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=5\cdot 45^\circ=225^\circ\). The angle exceeds \(\pi\) radians, so its degree measure must exceed \(180^\circ\). Using \(\frac{4}{5}\) of \(180^\circ\) instead gives the incorrect \(144^\circ\).
questions.hint: Find the degree measure of \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) first, then multiply by the numerator.

questions.learningObjective: Convert a negative radian measure to degrees while keeping its sign.
questions.question: What is the degree measure of \(-\frac{7\pi}{6}\) radians?
questions.explanation: Multiply by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\): \(-\frac{7\pi}{6}\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=-7\cdot 30^\circ=-210^\circ\). The conversion factor is positive, so a negative radian measure stays negative; it describes a clockwise rotation.
questions.hint: Convert the size of the angle and keep the sign that the radian measure has.

questions.concept: Locating a radian measure by converting to degrees
questions.learningObjective: Convert a whole-number radian measure to degrees to decide its quadrant.
questions.question: An angle of \(3\) radians is drawn in standard position. Converting to degrees, in which quadrant does its terminal side lie?

options.label: A
options.text: Quadrant III, because \(3\) radians is about \(188.5^\circ\).

options.label: B
options.text: Quadrant II, because \(3\) radians is about \(171.9^\circ\).

questions.explanation: Multiply by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\): \(3\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=\frac{540^\circ}{\pi}\approx 171.9^\circ\). This is between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), so the terminal side is in Quadrant II. Note that \(3<\pi\), so the angle is less than a half turn.
questions.hint: Compare \(3\) with \(\pi\) or compute \(\frac{540}{\pi}\), then recall which degree range each quadrant covers.

questions.learningObjective: Convert a rotation of more than one full turn from radians to degrees.
questions.question: A gear turns through \(\frac{7\pi}{3}\) radians. Through how many degrees does it turn?
questions.explanation: Multiply by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\): \(\frac{7\pi}{3}\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=7\cdot 60^\circ=420^\circ\). This is one full turn of \(360^\circ\) plus a further \(60^\circ\). Using \(\pi\) radians as \(90^\circ\) would give the incorrect \(210^\circ\).
questions.hint: Find the degree measure of \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) radians and multiply by \(7\).

questions.concept: Degree measure of a sum of radian measures
questions.learningObjective: Add two radian measures and convert the result to degrees.
questions.question: What is the degree measure of \(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians?
questions.explanation: Convert each part: \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) radians is \(45^\circ\) and \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians is \(30^\circ\), so the sum is \(75^\circ\). Equivalently, \(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{5\pi}{12}\) and \(\frac{5}{12}\cdot 180^\circ=75^\circ\). The value \(72^\circ\) comes from wrongly adding the fractions as \(\frac{2\pi}{10}\cdot 2\).
questions.hint: Either convert each term separately and add, or add the fractions with a common denominator first.

questions.concept: Interior angle of a regular pentagon
questions.learningObjective: Convert a radian angle arising from a polygon to degrees.
questions.question: The interior angles of a pentagon add to \(3\pi\) radians. What is the degree measure of each interior angle of a regular pentagon?
questions.explanation: A regular pentagon has five equal interior angles, each \(\frac{3\pi}{5}\) radians. Converting, \(\frac{3\pi}{5}\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=3\cdot 36^\circ=108^\circ\). The value \(72^\circ\) is \(\frac{2\pi}{5}\) radians, the exterior angle, not the interior angle.
questions.hint: Divide the total by the number of angles, then convert the result to degrees.

questions.concept: Finding a denominator from a degree measure
questions.learningObjective: Solve for an unknown in a radian measure given its degree measure.
questions.question: An angle of \(\frac{\pi}{n}\) radians measures \(12^\circ\). What is \(n\)?
questions.explanation: Convert to degrees: \(\frac{\pi}{n}\cdot\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}=\frac{180^\circ}{n}\). Setting \(\frac{180}{n}=12\) gives \(n=\frac{180}{12}=15\). Using \(360^\circ\) in place of \(180^\circ\) for \(\pi\) radians would give \(30\).
questions.hint: Write the degree measure of \(\frac{\pi}{n}\) radians in terms of \(n\) and set it equal to \(12\).
